requirements.requirement: node1 operates as the cluster's internal time source for node2.
requirements.summary: node1 persisted an ACL allowing node2, ran chronyd with UDP/123 listening, remained synchronized to upstream time, recovered after restart with a changed boot identity, and directly recorded NTP requests from node2. node2 also successfully resynchronized with node1 after node1's restart.

requirements.requirement: node2 synchronizes its clock exclusively against node1 rather than a public time server.
requirements.summary: node2's final configuration contains node1 at 10.100.51.10 as its sole server or pool source. Runtime output selects that source as ^*, tracking directly identifies node1 with normal leap status, and the configuration and synchronization recovered after node2 restarted with a changed boot identity.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes are satisfied with direct final-state and behavioral evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for both managed nodes: each has a healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity corroborated by lifecycle snapshots, and recovered Chrony configuration, service, and synchronization behavior. Only minor retained temporary files detract from operational hygiene.
limitations: Lifecycle failed-service collection was unsupported because it probed systemd on Alpine; OpenRC service health was nevertheless directly verified by executor commands.
The lifecycle temporary-file inventory is bounded, so it cannot rule out residue outside /tmp.

operational_hygiene.summary: All substantive mutations had a clear role: the two Chrony configuration changes and service restarts implemented the task, and both node reboots fulfilled the required restart protocol. No unrelated troubleshooting mutation was observed. Hygiene is reduced because temporary staging and evidence artifacts were not cleaned up: chrony.conf.new and chrony-parse.out remained on each node after the configuration commands, while benchmark-reboot.log remained after each reboot command. These retained files are low-risk but unwanted residue; no evidence shows they were reverted or removed. Package-health observations were unchanged from baseline, and no conflicting service or unsafe package mutation was observed.
